title: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.4 Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
intro: Choose bar charts or pie charts, interpret their scales, and compare categorical distributions fairly.

moments.title: Two displays
moments.text: Bar charts and pie charts display categorical data.

moments.title: Bar height
moments.text: Height or length represents a count or relative frequency.

moments.title: Equal bar widths
moments.text: Compare heights rather than changing the widths of bars.

moments.title: Estimate from a scale
moments.text: Read the axis before estimating category counts.

moments.title: Pie charts
moments.text: Slice areas represent fractions of the whole.

moments.title: Claims need evidence
moments.text: Use a displayed count or proportion to support a claim.

moments.title: Compare groups carefully
moments.text: Different group totals can reverse a comparison of counts and proportions.

moments.title: Tree species example
moments.text: Read approximate species counts from a sample of 300 trees.

moments.title: Convert counts to proportions
moments.text: Divide estimated counts by the known sample total.

cards.name: Bar chart
cards.text: Use a common baseline, equal widths, category labels, and a count or proportion scale.

cards.name: Pie chart
cards.text: Use disjoint categories that account for the whole; slices total 100%.

cards.name: Different group sizes
cards.text: Compare proportions when the question concerns the share in each category.

cards.name: Graph readings
cards.text: Treat readings from an unlabeled bar as estimates, not exact counts.

questions.obj: Estimate a proportion from a bar chart
questions.q: The video shows a sample of 300 Ohio trees. The elm bar is approximately 25 trees. Estimate the percentage of sampled trees that are elms.

work.text: The axis shows counts, and the elm bar is approximately 25.

steps.t: Divide by the total sample size.

work.text: The estimate inherits the uncertainty of reading the bar.

questions.answer: Approximately 8.3% of the sampled trees are elms.

traps.title: Counts versus shares
traps.weak: A taller count bar always means a larger percentage.
traps.better: Compare category counts relative to their own group totals.

traps.title: Unsupported precision
traps.better: The unlabeled bar appears to represent approximately 25 trees.

traps.title: A pie with overlap
traps.better: Pie slices must form disjoint parts of one whole.

traps.title: Drawing a chart
traps.weak: Technology means construction is not a required skill.
traps.better: Know how to label axes, choose a scale, and represent the counts or proportions correctly.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Constructing categorical graphs is a CED learning objective. The video downplays drawing them by hand; this page retains the construction requirements.

questions.stem: Club A has 30 cyclists among 50 members. Club B has 48 among 120. Which is true?
opts: A has more cyclists and a higher proportion
A has a higher proportion, but B has more cyclists
why: A has 60% and B has 40%, while 48 exceeds 30.

questions.stem: Which is essential for a conventional bar chart of counts?
opts: A common zero baseline and a labeled count scale
Bars ordered numerically by category name
why: A common zero baseline lets lengths represent counts fairly.
Category names have no required numerical order.

questions.stem: A pie chart slice represents one quarter of the area. What does it establish?
opts: The category count exceeds every other count
why: A quarter of the area represents one quarter of the observations.
Four equal quarters do not imply four individuals.

questions.stem: A chart records which sports students play; students may choose several. Why is an ordinary pie chart unsuitable?
opts: The responses overlap and do not partition students
why: Color is not the mathematical issue.
One student can belong to several categories, so slices are not disjoint parts of the whole.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: At two campuses, students report one main lunch choice. Campus A: packed 48, cafeteria 24, other 8. Campus B: packed 60, cafeteria 90, other 50.
parts: (a) Specify how to construct comparable relative frequency bar charts.
(b) Compare packed-lunch choices using counts and percentages.
(c) Explain why the counts alone give a different impression.
sample: (a) Use the same categories and a common percentage scale starting at zero. For A, plot 60%, 30%, and 10%; for B, plot 30%, 45%, and 25%, with equal-width bars and clear labels.
(b) Campus B has more packed lunches, 60 versus 48. Campus A has the larger share, 60% versus 30%.
(c) The campus totals differ: A has 80 students and B has 200. Relative frequencies account for those unequal totals.
checklist: Specifies a common labeled percentage scale.
Explains the effect of different totals.
